one_liner: Header-only AVX2 hash-count sort for integer vectors with few distinct values; beats pdqsort, IPS4o and vqsort while K stays far below N.
what_it_does: Sorts a std::vector of integers ascending by counting how often each distinct value occurs and rewriting the vector from the sorted (value, count) list, so it only pays off when the number of distinct values K is much smaller than N. The API is cafs2::cafs_sort(std::vector<T>&, fallback): no iterator, span, comparator or payload interface, and an optional fallback callable (default std::sort) handles inputs the dispatcher rejects. Thin C, Python (NumPy), Rust and Go wrappers expose a sort for uint64, int64 and int32 by copying into a temporary vector and back.
how_it_is_fast: A dispatcher first returns early on already-sorted input (and reverses non-increasing input), then estimates K with the Chao1 estimator over 1024 strided samples. For K of 8 or fewer it makes one branchless pass counting matches against eight candidate keys; otherwise each run of equal values is hashed (Fibonacci multiplicative hash) into a table of 64-byte, cache-line-aligned buckets (4 u64/i64 or 8 i32 keys plus 32-bit counts) probed with one AVX2 cmpeq plus movemask, sized to about 8 slots per estimated key. Keys that find their bucket full go to a spill vector sorted with std::sort; the distinct (key, count) pairs are LSD-radix-sorted and expanded with fill_n, so the work is O(N + K) instead of O(N log N). If the sample looks all-unique, K_est * 2 > N, or the spill exceeds N/2, the input goes to the fallback.
when_to_use: Large (N of 1e5 and up) uint64, int64 or int32 columns with K far below N: dictionary-encoded or categorical fields, foreign keys into small dimension tables, bucketed numeric features; the README bins show 1.27-2.34x vqsort and 2.1-3.1x pdqsort for K up to about 16,384
Arrays with 8 or fewer distinct values, where the single counting pass measured 17.1x libstdc++ std::sort and 3.1x pdqsort
x86-64 machines with AVX2 but no AVX-512 (the measured i5-12400F class), where vqsort is also limited to its AVX2 path
Cases where only the sorted integers are needed (no satellite data) and you can pass pdqsort as the fallback so high-cardinality inputs degrade to pdqsort speed rather than std::sort
when_not_to_use: K that may approach N: for N above 1e6 vqsort wins by 1.5-2x past K of about 6.7e5, ska_sort wins past 8.1e5, and the worst case seen in the grid was about 5x pdqsort time

Sorting records, key-value pairs, floats, custom orders or anything other than a std::vector of integers: output is regenerated from counts, so it cannot carry payloads or act as a general std::sort replacement

Non-x86 or pre-AVX2 targets: there is no runtime dispatch (binaries built with -mavx2 fault on older CPUs), and <immintrin.h> is included unconditionally, so the header does not build on ARM even for types that use the scalar bucket path

Memory-tight code: the table holds about two 64-byte buckets per estimated distinct key, capped at bit_ceil(N/4) buckets (up to about twice the size of a u64 input), plus the spill vector, the (key, count) array and a radix buffer

Production code that needs a track record: one author, 7 commits between 2026-05-09 and 2026-08-07, no releases, no filed issues, all numbers from one Windows desktop, and the preprint is not peer reviewed

integration.dependencies: none for the library (include/cafs.hpp and include/cafs2.hpp); the benchmark needs pdqsort.h and optionally ska_sort, IPS4o (with TBB headers or stubs) and Google Highway
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (std::bit_ceil, std::bit_width, std::countr_zero); g++ 13+ or clang 16+ per the README; MSVC not documented
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 and BMI1 only (compile with -mavx2 -mbmi); Windows (_aligned_malloc) and POSIX (std::aligned_alloc) allocation paths
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each call allocates its own table and touches only the vector passed in, so concurrent calls on different vectors look safe from the code; the sort itself is single-threaded
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()) on a std::vector of integers in ascending order only; no iterator, comparator or payload interface

gotchas: The default fallback is std::sort, but the benchmark passes pdqsort (main_bigdata.cpp), and the C, Python, Rust and Go bindings call the default. Past the dispatcher's cutoff the measured CAFS is pdqsort (bin-mean 1.00), whereas default and binding users get std::sort, which the same table puts 3.47x slower in the K = 8.4e6-1.7e7 bin (derived from page data). Pass pdqsort or vqsort as the fallback explicitly.

Harness gaps found this session: competitors.hpp implements dense_map_sort (count with ankerl::unordered_dense, sort the distinct keys, expand), which is the plain hash-count-sort that CAFS's technique should be compared against, and Boost spreadsort, but main_bigdata.cpp never registers either, so the published table only pits an O(N + K log K) histogram method against comparison and radix sorts. The 592,770 rows are exactly the driver's default grid truncated at N = 3e7 (98,795 (N, K) cases x 6 algorithms over 58 sizes, best of 2 each; the preprint abstract, seen as a search snippet, also says 58 sizes), not a 1600-point grid, so the 3.5e7-1e8 sizes were not part of the published run. The heatmap script silently drops rows whose output check failed and the CSV is unpublished, so FAIL rows cannot be ruled out.

The K estimate reads every (N/1024)-th element, so periodic inputs alias: with N = 1,048,576 and data[i] = key[i % 1024] the sample sees one value, the table is sized at its 8-bucket minimum (32 slots), about 97% of the elements are pushed into a spill vector reserved for 8, and the fallback then sorts everything anyway (read from the code, not run). Skewed (Zipf-like) inputs were not benchmarked; every grid point draws keys uniformly from the palette.

Hashing is a bare Fibonacci multiply into 4-slot buckets with no rehash, and spilled keys are sorted with std::sort rather than the fallback. My Python simulation of the table fill with the benchmark's own arithmetic-progression palette at K = 100,000 spilled 4,635 keys against 18 for random 64-bit keys, so structured key sets can spill far more than the measured ones. Counts are 32-bit (wraps only past 2^32 copies of one value), and the older cafs::cafs_sort entry point in cafs.hpp, still reachable through cafs2.hpp, returns with the data unsorted if its table allocation fails.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick CAFS over vqsort, pdqsort, IPS4o or ska_sort only for integer-only sorts on AVX2 hardware where K is known to stay well below about 1e5 (the pdqsort crossover) to 6.7e5 (the vqsort crossover). Pick vqsort (Highway) when K may approach N or you need AVX-512, NEON or SVE dispatch, and pdqsort for portable general-purpose sorting; no comparison with x86-simd-sort exists.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run grid on an Intel Core i5-12400F under Windows 11 (g++ 13.2 -O3 -mavx2 -mbmi, libstdc++ std::sort, vqsort on its AVX2 path): uint64 keys drawn uniformly from K-value palettes, N from 1,000 to 3e7, best of 2 runs per point, with CAFS using a pdqsort fallback. Bin-mean speedups are 17.1x std::sort, 3.1x pdqsort and 1.32x vqsort at K = 4-8, still 1.59x vqsort at K of about 1e4, and fall to 0.60x vqsort and 0.66x ska_sort near K = N; every output is checked against std::sort, so the timings are of real sorts.
status_note: Active but young (single author, 7 commits from 2026-05-09 to 2026-08-07, 32 stars, no releases or issues); MIT and two small headers, so easy to vendor, best used behind your own K check with an explicit pdqsort or vqsort fallback.
